description: Artificial intelligence and new forms of employment are shaking a model of work inherited from the industrial age.

hero.hook: Machines work faster than ever. The question is what will be left for humans to do.

blocks.text: Work does not only decide our income: it also shapes our social identity and the meaning we give our days. Artificial intelligence, robotics and new ways of working are now shaking that model, inherited from the industrial age.
This course explores how work is changing shape, and the big questions that transformation raises: fewer hours, more machines, and a new way of sharing wealth.

Modern work was long organized around an idea made popular by **[[Henry Ford]]**, who introduced the 40-hour week in 1926. It was not a gesture of generosity: workers with free time also become customers, able to buy the products they build themselves.

In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that his grandchildren would work only 15 hours a week, thanks to technical progress. Almost a century later we have that technology, and we still work just as much.

The model is crumbling today in favor of the **gig economy**, work paid by the task: more than 57 million workers in the United States now sell their services through digital platforms, outside classic employment. Automation is taking on more and more complex tasks too, while remote work, accelerated by the 2020 pandemic, is redrawing the very geography of work.

sections.title: The end of the model born with Henry Ford

blocks.text: Debate about the future of work often leans on an idea from the philosopher and economist **[[Joseph Schumpeter]]**: **[[Creative destruction]]**. For him, every technological revolution destroys old trades but ends up creating new ones, often more skilled. Generative artificial intelligence brings something new, though: for the first time it threatens office jobs and professions seen as intellectual.
In 2023, a study found that artificial intelligence scored better than 99% of humans on a creativity test, casting doubt on the idea that creativity is our last advantage over machines.

Three scenarios are taking shape. The optimistic one imagines a rise in productivity that frees people from repetitive tasks. The pessimistic one fears that AI will advance faster than our ability to retrain, creating mass unemployment. The hybrid one bets on collaboration between human and machine, where the key skill becomes the ability to direct the tools rather than to master a fixed craft.

sections.title: AI and the challenge of creative destruction

blocks.text: Faced with the risk of a two-speed society, new tools are under study. **Universal basic income** would pay a fixed sum to every citizen, with no conditions, to secure people's lives in an economy where work is becoming more intermittent.

blocks.caption: Automation, artificial intelligence and new forms of employment are redrawing the world of work

blocks.text: Alongside it, the idea of a **[[4-day week]]** is gaining ground: if machines produce more in less time, it seems logical that human working hours should fall in return, to protect jobs and workers' health. That leaves the question of funding: if value is more and more created by software, taxes will probably have to shift from income earned by labor to income earned by capital.

Once the economic equation is solved, a deeper question remains: what becomes of the meaning of our days in a world where work matters less? Historically, work has structured daily life and self-esteem. Its partial disappearance could lead either to boredom or to a revival of volunteer, artistic and civic activity.
The French word for work, travail, comes from the Latin tripalium, an instrument of torture with three stakes. An origin that recalls how long work was seen as suffering before it became an identity.

In that context, learning how to learn becomes an essential skill. The real issue is not only technological but political: will we use artificial intelligence to expand what people can do, or only to cut company costs? The answer will decide whether tomorrow's work is a liberation or a new constraint.

The future of work is marked by the end of the single salaried job, giving way to the gig economy, and by the challenge of artificial intelligence, which for the first time threatens intellectual jobs. Our social model will probably have to redistribute the gains in productivity, through a universal income or a shorter working week.

sections.title: What meaning to give the work of tomorrow
